**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Our macOS pre-merge jobs are non-blocking. Often maintainers will merge over a pending macOS check, either because it's irrelevant to the current change, or a previous revision has already passed on macOS, etc. During the busy parts of the day, the PR job can get stuck in the queue behind others, thus not actually running until after the PR has already been merged. At that point the job becomes completely irrelevant (if it failed, continuous would flag a failure), but our Jenkins doesn't currently understand that.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

At the beginning of an experimental (pre-merge) job, Jenkins would be able to recognize if the current drake revision being tested has already been merged, and in that case, abort the job. Preferably abort with 'success' status, so we don't get spurious failure statuses reported back to GitHub.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

n/a

**Additional context**

n/a
new_candidates.title: [ci] Avoid running redundant macOS PR jobs after merge

## Feature request

#### Feature description

On long global plans, `controller_server`'s own per-cycle work grows linearly with the number of poses still ahead of the robot. It does so regardless of the controller plugin. Two places do it:

1. **Pruning in `FeasiblePathHandler`.** `FeasiblePathHandler::transformLocalPlan()` prunes the passed poses every cycle with `prunePlan()`, i.e. `plan.poses.erase(plan.poses.begin(), closest_point)` (`nav2_controller/plugins/feasible_path_handler.cpp`, still on `main`). Erasing the front of a `std::vector<PoseStamped>` moves every remaining pose. So each cycle that the closest pose advances, the whole rest of the plan is moved.
2. **`remaining_path_length` in the tracking feedback.** `ControllerServer::computeAndPublishVelocity()` recomputes `tracking_feedback_msg->remaining_path_length = calculate_path_length(current_path_, start_index_)` every cycle (`nav2_controller/src/controller_server.cpp`). That walks every remaining pose.

This matters for coverage paths. A coverage plan for a ~2000 m² lawn at 3 cm pose spacing is a single `FollowPath` goal of ~400k poses; 600–1200 m² areas give 80k–220k.

**Measurement.**
- Setup: Nav2 1.5.2 (Lyrical, apt binaries), x86-64 i7-10700K, one pinned core.
- What runs: the real `FeasiblePathHandler` plugin and the `nav2_util` functions, called in the order `ControllerServer` calls them each cycle (`findPlanSegment` + `transformLocalPlan`, then `distance_from_path` + `calculate_path_length`). Shipped defaults otherwise, with `max_robot_pose_search_dist: 10.0`.
- Robot on the path, advancing 5 cm per cycle. Medians of 21 runs × 200 cycles.

| poses ahead | path handler | `calculate_path_length` | total per cycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10k | 70 µs | 47 µs | 119 µs |
| 50k | 434 µs | 361 µs | 798 µs |
| 100k | 931 µs | 764 µs | 1.71 ms |
| 200k | 1.92 ms | 1.55 ms | 3.51 ms |
| 400k | 3.95 ms | 3.10 ms | 7.21 ms |

That is ~18 ns per remaining pose per cycle. At 400k poses it is comparable to the controller plugin itself; our controller takes ~8 ms per cycle on the same machine, independent of path length. Both loops stream the whole remaining plan through memory every cycle, so the cost should be noticeably higher on ARM SBCs such as a Raspberry Pi; we have not measured that yet.

#### Implementation considerations

1. **Pruning: track an offset instead of erasing every cycle.**
   - Keep the passed prefix of `global_plan_up_to_constraint_` in place behind an index. Start `findPlanSegment`'s searches at `begin() + offset`. Erase in bulk only once the passed prefix is more than half the vector. That is O(1) amortized, and results are identical to today's.
   - The `enforce_path_inversion` / `enforce_path_rotation` branch reassigns the pruned plan, so it should compact first.
   - The two size checks (`transformToGlobalPlanFrame`, and the "don't prune below 2 poses" guard) should use the logical size. Today they cannot differ, because pruning never leaves fewer than 2 poses.
   - A `std::deque` would avoid the bookkeeping, but `nav2_core::PathIterator` is a public `std::vector` iterator type.
   - We implemented this as a subclass of `FeasiblePathHandler`. We checked it against the upstream plugin side by side, cycle by cycle: returned segment, transformed local plan, exceptions, transformed goal and the pruned plan itself. The checks covered closed loops, plans leaving the costmap, replans, 1–3 pose plans and an inversion cusp with `enforce_path_inversion` on. The handler's per-cycle cost became flat: 8–14 µs from 1k to 400k poses, versus 3.95 ms at 400k.
2. **`remaining_path_length`: compute it once per plan.**
   - Build a cumulative-length table once in `setPlannerPath()`, and report `total - prefix[start_index_]`. That is O(1) per cycle.
   - The summation order differs from today's, so the value can differ in the last bits. It only feeds `TrackingFeedback`.

Happy to open a PR for either or both if this direction is welcome.
new_candidates.title: controller_server: per-cycle cost grows linearly with remaining plan length (FeasiblePathHandler prune erase, remaining_path_length)

**Expected Behavior**:

The test passes reliably, or the timing tolerance accounts for scheduler jitter on Windows CI machines.

**Actual Behavior**:

`RosBag2PlayTestFixture.high_freq_topics_does_not_starve_in_multibag_playback` (`rosbag2_transport/test/rosbag2_transport/test_play.cpp`) fails flaky on Windows. The test plays three bags and checks that the wall-clock interval between consecutive published messages per topic stays within `period / 2` of the expected period. For the high frequency topic (period 20 ms) the accepted window is 10 to 30 ms. In failing runs some intervals are above the window (33 to 43 ms) and others are 0 ms (bursts).

It failed on every `nightly_win_rep` build from `#4281` to `#4286` (some builds in only one of the two RMW variants).

## To Reproduce
This is flaky test regression observed on [nightly_win_rep](https://ci.ros2.org/job/nightly_win_rep):
1. On Windows, build rosbag2 from source on the `rolling` branch.
2. Run the test repeatedly:
   ```
   colcon test --packages-select rosbag2_transport --ctest-args -R test_play --event-handlers console_direct+
   ```
   3. Check for `time_diff` assertion failures at `test_play.cpp(894)`.

## System (please complete the following information)
 - OS: Windows Server container (Docker image built with `WINDOWS_RELEASE_VERSION=10.0.20348.2227`), agent `windows-container-4073262f`
 - ROS 2 Distro: Rolling
 - Install Method: Source (ros2/ci job `nightly_win_rep`)
 - Version: rosbag2 at `rolling`. RMW: the `rmw_cyclonedds_cpp` and `rmw_fastrtps_cpp` variants of the test fail, `rmw_zenoh_cpp` passes.

</details>

  Actual: 33 (of type __int64), which doesn't match (is <= 30)

[  FAILED  ] RosBag2PlayTestFixture.high_freq_topics_does_not_starve_in_multibag_playback (1164 ms)
```

<details><summary>Test source (rolling), timing check</summary>

```
// Allow for a tolerance of high_freq_topic_period_ms / 2 = 10 ms
const rcutils_duration_value_t tolerance_ms = high_freq_topic_period_ms / 2;  // 10 ms;
...
auto time_diff = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(
  published_msgs[i].first - published_msgs[i - 1].first).count();
EXPECT_THAT(time_diff,
            AllOf(Ge(high_freq_topic_period_ms - tolerance_ms),
                  Le(high_freq_topic_period_ms + tolerance_ms))
) << "msg_number=" << i << ", time_diff=" << time_diff;

### Analysis notes
- Values are both too high (33 to 43 ms) and 0, which looks like scheduling jitter and bunching, not a fixed offset.
- Each build also logs `Message queue starved` warnings (52 to 55 per build for `#4281` to `#4286`), so that warning is baseline and not specific to a failing build.
- Hypothesis: the 10 ms tolerance is too tight for loaded Windows CI containers because the check depends on wall-clock scheduling.
